query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing chromium content in steel enhances the formation and stability of a passivating oxide layer at high temperature and pressure, thereby reducing corrosion in chemical-processing and nuclear-reactor environments.
generation.material_initial_state: Low-alloy and high-chromium steels, solution-annealed, with systematically varied chromium content in a range typical for stainless steels (e.g., 9–18% Cr).
generation.intervention: Expose the steels in a high-temperature (up to ~300 °C), pressurized aqueous environment doped with representative corrosive species (e.g., chloride and lithium hydroxide, simulating chemical and nuclear conditions) while maintaining a neutral or slightly alkaline pH.
generation.conditions: Controlled autoclave tests under ~10–12 MPa pressure, up to 300–320 °C, O2 < 10 ppm, with repeated 20- or 40-day intervals of immersion, complemented by ex situ analysis.
generation.structural_mediator: Chromium-enriched oxide film, formed on the steel surface under these high-temperature, corrosive environments.
generation.mechanism: Cr2O3-rich passivation layers reduce metal dissolution by limiting oxygen and aggressive ion transport between the environment and underlying steel.
generation.predicted_outcome: Steel grades with higher chromium concentrations will show consistently larger charge-transfer resistances (by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy) and lower corrosion currents (by potentiodynamic polarization) compared to lower-chromium baseline steels. Surface analysis will indicate more continuous, uniform, Cr-rich oxide layers on high-chromium steels after repeated exposures.
generation.baseline: Low-alloy steel (≤ 5% Cr content) tested under identical conditions, which will exhibit higher corrosion rates and a less protective oxide layer.
generation.boundary: Valid primarily for ferritic, martensitic, and austenitic steels with chromium contents between 9% and 18%, tested in high-temperature pressurized water with controlled chemistry typical of chemical processing or nuclear primary circuits. Does not cover extreme acid or extremely oxidizing conditions beyond these ranges.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of passivation improvement may vary among specific steel compositions, microstructures, and test conditions; other alloying elements (e.g., Ni, Mo) and local pH variations could also influence corrosion processes.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare multiple steel specimens with incremental chromium contents in a high-temperature, high-pressure water loop containing controlled amounts of corrosive ions. Perform multiple 20–40 day immersion cycles, analyzing oxide morphology and chemical composition after each cycle.
measurements: Potentiodynamic polarization curves to measure corrosion current densities
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy to measure charge-transfer resistance
Surface characterization (e.g., SEM, XPS) to confirm presence/chemistry of Cr-rich oxide layers
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If steels with increased chromium content do not show significant improvement in corrosion resistance or if no selective chromium-rich passivation layer is detected, then the hypothesis is invalidated.

cited_evidence.text: The corrosion test was carried out in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution. An electrolytic cell with a size of 2 × 2 × 0.5 cm3 could fix the specimen, which ensured that the test area was 1 cm2. The surface was polished and cleaned with alcohol, acetone and deionized water. The polarization experiments were performed in a Potentiostat Workstation (CHI600E). All the experiments were carried out in a standard three-electrode cell system including a reference electrode of Ag/AgCl (3M KCl) solid electrode and an auxiliary electrode of a platinum sheet. The HEAC was a working electrode. During the experiment, the working electrode was corroded for 3600 s to acquire a quasistationary value of the open-circuit potential (OCP). Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was carried out at OCP with an amplitude perturbation voltage of 10 mV (peak to peak) and a frequency ranging from 100 kHz to 10 MHz. The potentiodynamic-polarization tests were carried out at a scan rate of 100 mV/min from an initial potential of 0.25 V vs. OCP, and stopped at the end when the current density increased to 1 mA/cm2. Immersion tests were performed in the 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at room temperature for 240 h.

For the chemical analysis of the geothermal fluid in wells HE-23 and HE-56, sampling and analysis of the liquid and condensable gas (gas that was condensed and analyzed in liquid state) and gaseous species in the fluid had to be conducted separately. Sampling and analysis of the liquid were only conducted from the aerated pressure vessel. The test conditions and chemical analysis (of the most corrosive species) of the fluids from the three locations can be viewed in Table 2 and the testing periods in Table 3, respectively.

A static autoclave was used to conduct the corrosion test. To simulate the solution environment under service conditions, an aqueous solution containing 1000 ppm of HBO3 and 3.5 ppm of LiOH (by weight) was prepared with pure water and injected into the reactor, with O content restricted to less than 10 ppm (by volume). The instrument’s working pressure was set to 11.3 MPa, the temperature was set to 320 °C, and the heating rate was set to 6 °C/min. After 20 days of corrosion, it was naturally cooled, and a group of samples was removed. The remaining samples were left in the autoclave, and the temperature was raised using the same parameters. Another bunch of samples from the autoclave was taken out after 20 days. The process was repeated 3 times to obtain water corrosion samples with exposure times of 20, 40, and 60 days. After removing the samples, they were washed with deionized water and dried with nitrogen for analysis.
